incumbent.name: Zach Payne
incumbent.summary: Zach Payne, a Republican from Charlestown, was elected in 2020 and is vice chair of the House Elections and Apportionment Committee; he also serves on the Education and Employment, Labor and Pensions committees, according to the House Republican caucus {payne_bio}. He previously served as Clark County recorder and on the Jeffersonville City Council from 2012 to 2015 {payne_bio}.
record: December 2024: Reappointed vice chair of the House Elections and Apportionment Committee, saying "Fair, secure elections are a cornerstone of Indiana's democratic process" {payne_committees_2024}.
January 2024: Welcomed Meta's planned data center at River Ridge Commerce Center in Jeffersonville, saying "Southern Indiana continues to be a major player in economic development" {payne_meta}.

On April 10, 2025, voted for SB 1, the property-tax and local government finance bill, which passed the House 65–29 {rc_sb1_433}. On April 25, 2025, voted for the conference report on HEA 1001, the 2025–2027 state budget, adopted 66–27 {rc_hb1001_576}.
December 5, 2025: Voted for HB 1032, the mid-decade congressional redistricting bill, which passed the House 57–41 {rc_hb1032_28}.
February 19, 2026: Voted to concur in Senate changes to HB 1002, the electric utility affordability bill (94–2) {rc_hb1002_293}.
January 2026: Authored HB 1422 on immigration matters and HB 1376 on prohibited food additives; both were referred to committee with no further action listed {pr_hb1422} {pr_hb1376}.
2021–2022: Co-authored the early-voting expansion law (2021) and authored the 2022 House version of handgun carry without a license, according to the caucus {payne_bio}.

race_context: House District 66 includes portions of Clark, Jefferson and Scott counties in southern Indiana, according to the House Republican caucus {payne_bio}.
Payne won the seat in 2020 by defeating Democratic incumbent Terry Goodin 55.8% to 44.2%, and was re-elected in 2024 with 69.4% of the vote, according to Wikipedia {wiki_payne} {wiki_2026_inhouse}.
Payne and Price are each listed by Wikipedia as the only declared candidates in their parties' May 5, 2026 primaries {wiki_2026_inhouse}.
No debate or forum between the two candidates was found as of October 10, 2026.

Data centers are a local issue: Payne praised Meta's Jeffersonville data center in 2024, while Price calls for state rules on where and how data centers are built and for tighter regulation of related tax exemptions {payne_meta} {price_site}.

candidates.summary: Ryan Price, the Democratic nominee, describes himself as a working Hoosier who has held blue-collar and office jobs and volunteered on fundraising, budgeting and safety projects {price_site}.
background: Says he has worked in both blue-collar and office jobs and has volunteered on fundraising, budgeting and safety projects {price_site}.
Discussed housing, education and local leadership in a January 2026 interview with The Recovered Republican, a Substack publication {substack_price}.
path_to_ballot: Wikipedia lists him as the only declared candidate in the May 5, 2026 Democratic primary {wiki_2026_inhouse}.

items: Opposes public money going to private schools and supports fully funding public schools, citing more than $490 million moved to private schools in 2024–2025 {price_site}.
Says wages have not kept pace with housing, health care, child care and grocery costs, and supports workers' rights {price_site}.
Supports affordable care and keeping rural medical facilities open {price_site}.
Proposes property assessment reform, incentives for modest energy-efficient starter homes, and protections against large corporate purchases of first-time-buyer homes {price_site}.

Proposes a marginal income tax structure that lowers the burden on working and middle-class families, and tighter regulation of corporate tax incentives such as exemptions for large data center projects {price_site}.

Supports solar on existing structures rather than farmland; wants laws on where and how data centers are built rather than stopping the industry, and wants to end AI tracking of citizens {price_site}.

on_incumbent: His campaign site does not mention Payne {price_site}.
plans: Lists education, wages, health care, housing, tax reform and solar/data center rules as priorities {price_site}.
endorsements_finance: No endorsements are listed on his campaign site, which takes donations through ActBlue {price_site}.
gaps: No local news coverage of his campaign was found.
The Ballot Brief reported no campaign website as of Sept. 8, 2026, though pricein66.com was live on Oct. 10.

candidates.summary: The Republican incumbent, first elected in 2020 and vice chair of the House Elections and Apportionment Committee {payne_bio}.
background: Owns a marketing business in southern Indiana; holds degrees from Purdue University, the University of Southern Indiana and Charter Oak State College, according to the caucus {payne_bio}.
Served as Clark County recorder and on the Jeffersonville City Council (2012–2015) {payne_bio}.
path_to_ballot: Wikipedia lists him as the only declared candidate in the May 5, 2026 Republican primary {wiki_2026_inhouse}.

items: His campaign site cites his votes for what it calls the largest tax cut in state history and the $545 million automatic taxpayer refund {payne_site}.
Says he co-authored the law allowing handgun carry without a license {payne_site}.
His site describes a "100% pro-life voting record" {payne_site}.
Says he is focused on helping southern Indiana attract higher-paying jobs {payne_site}.
Said in 2024 that "we will continue to pursue ways to ensure all Hoosiers can vote in the safest way possible" {payne_committees_2024}.

on_incumbent: Is the current officeholder. No statements by Payne about his challenger were found {payne_site}.
plans: His campaign site lists support for taxpayers, higher-paying jobs and local law enforcement {payne_site}.
endorsements_finance: No formal endorsements are listed on his campaign site {payne_site}.
gaps: The caucus member page lists no Payne press releases dated 2026.
No public statements explaining his votes on SB 1, the 2025 budget or HB 1032 were found; Louisville Public Media noted his vote for HB 1032 without comment from him.
His role in the House Elections Committee's December 2025 handling of HB 1032 was not confirmed.
Wikipedia says he was endorsed in 2024 by Ron Paul and Rep. Thomas Massie; 2026 endorsements not found.
